1	# Task 11: Solar-system explorer with focus on click
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. The app is an interactive, stylised solar system explorer on a dark starfield background.
4	
5	Show a glowing central star and at least 6 planets, each at a different orbital distance, with a different size and colour and orbiting the star at a different speed (inner planets faster). At least one planet has a moon orbiting it, and at least one planet has a ring. Draw a thin circular orbit line for each planet. Planets should also spin about their own axis. Use a simple procedural look (colour, gradients or generated textures); do not load external assets from the network.
6	
7	The user can click a planet to focus on it. On focus, the camera smoothly moves (about 1.5 seconds, eased) to a close view of that planet and keeps following it as it orbits, and a DOM info panel appears showing the planet's name, its orbital period in Earth days, and its distance from the star in million km. Clicking empty space, or pressing the Escape key, smoothly returns to the overview showing the whole system and hides the panel. In the overview, the user can drag to orbit the camera around the system and scroll to zoom within sensible limits. Add a toggle button labelled 'Pause' that stops and resumes orbital motion, and shows 'Play' while paused.
8	
9	The scene must look correct on first load with no console errors. Expose

Without a way to actually run and verify behavior, I should look more carefully at the extension code to see exactly how the app exposes camera and whether the update loop invokes it properly.

This setup works fine — I'll set the camera via setPose each frame with position/target, letting overrides apply after the rig updates, with default up vector. For picking, I'll implement my own ray computation from the camera pose and mouse coordinates, intersecting with a known sphere.

I need to build rays using forward/right/up vectors with vertical FOV matching the perspective matrix, then do ray-sphere intersection with slightly enlarged radii for easier picking on small planets, sorted by nearest hit. I'll use getBoundingClientRect for canvas coordinates, distinguish clicks from drags by movement threshold (under 4px counts as a click), and handle interactions differently depending on whether I'm in overview or focus mode — dragging orbits the camera in overview, clicking elsewhere unfocuses, clicking another planet switches focus, and wheel zooms.

For camera state, I'm tracking yaw/pitch/distance/target for overview mode and computing focus-mode position as an offset from the planet, with smooth eased transitions over 1.5s between start and end poses whenever focus changes.

For transitions, I'm defining a generic desiredPose() function depending on mode, blending linearly with easing from the currently presented pose to the target, and restarting the transition timer if the user refocuses mid-transition. I'm computing camera-to-focus distance using the live presented camera position, and setting `focused` immediately on click. For the focus camera offset, I'm placing the camera along a direction outward from the planet rotated slightly upward, at a distance scaled to the planet's radius, and defining overall scene scale constants for star radius, planet distances, and planet radii, with the overview camera positioned at a fixed default distance and far clipping plane.

For following the planet, I want the camera offset to be fixed relative to the planet's radial direction from the star so the lit side stays visible as it orbits—combining a radial inward component with a tangential component and slight elevation, normalized and scaled by distance, so the camera smoothly orbits along with the planet.

For moons and rings, I'm thinking through implementation: moon distance scaled to planet radius so it's partially visible in frame, ringed planets needing a wider camera distance. Positions update each frame by computing orbital angles and setting each node's position and spin rotation, with moons and rings as separate child nodes offset from the planet. For rings specifically, I'm considering building a custom flat annulus geometry rather than relying on uncertain primitive options, and making sure the material renders both faces so the ring doesn't disappear from certain viewing angles.

For the ring's coloring, I want radial gradient bands using vertex colors across the ring's width, interpolated smoothly between segments. For orbit paths, I'm weighing custom line geometry against a thin flattened torus or a narrow triangle-strip ring, considering visibility at typical camera distances and frame resolution.

Given the pixel-size math at distance 120, something like 0.12 units wide risks sub-pixel aliasing, so I'll bump orbit line width to roughly 0.18-0.2 units with an emissive, unlit-leaning material so they stay visibly thin but not invisible at a glance. I still need to check what fields the material spec actually exposes (emissive, emissiveIntensity, roughness, metallic, map, side) to pin down how to render these rings convincingly.

Now I'm also considering whether there are preset material helpers like a planet preset or sun/corona presets that could save me from building this from scratch, so I want to look at those definitions before committing.

content.thinking:
I'm thinking the sun needs a shader material plus a corona layer for glow, and for planets I want procedural GLSL shading with bands or noise so the spin is visible, lit by direction toward the star using world position from the model matrix.

I'm baking colors directly into each planet's shader string rather than using uniforms to keep things simple, and confirming that local-space position (not world) should drive the pattern so it rotates naturally with spin, while checking that rotation values use small radian units consistent with other examples.

For the sun, I'm leaning toward a custom emissive GLSL shader with noise and output brightness above 1 for bloom, rather than relying on an unknown built-in solar shader, plus a larger additive-blended fresnel shell for the glow effect.

For the glow halo, I'm working out the fresnel falloff math: since the glow sphere sits 1.5× the sun's radius, the dot(n,v) value at the sun's silhouette edge works out to about 0.745, so I need the glow intensity to fall off appropriately from that threshold outward using a power curve on dot(n,v).

Since transparent objects draw after opaque ones, the glow shell's front face will render additively over the sun itself where they overlap on screen, creating a bright white highlight — that's fine since bloom will handle it, and I can scale the additive color by the fresnel term to keep it from overpowering. Clicking the sun itself should just count as clicking empty space, which unfocuses any selection.

For the starfield, I'm considering representing stars as instanced tiny spheres distributed on a large distant sphere using an emissive white material.
